Flipping Items Simultaneously III

AlgorithmsParityNumber Theory
Game: A ring of red circles must all be turned blue, with as few clicks as you can manage.
How to play: Press a circle: it and the next few circles clockwise swap colours. Choose how many with M, and how many circles with N. Tick Show the answer to check the fewest clicks.

Look for the math

There are N lights in a circle, all off, and a click toggles M neighbouring ones. In Levitin’s puzzle M = 3. What is the fewest clicks that turn every light on?

The answer

Let g = gcd(M, N), M₁ = M/g and N₁ = N/g. The puzzle can be solved exactly when M₁ is odd, and then N₁ clicks are the fewest: click every gth circle. When M divides N, that is N/M clicks. When M₁ is even there is no way at all. The logic test tried every set of circles to click, for every N up to 20 and every M, and the fewest it found was the page’s N₁ each time, or none when M₁ is even. It also solved the equations for every pair with N up to 60.

Why one click per circle is enough

A circle’s colour depends only on how many times it has been flipped, not on the order, and two clicks on the same circle cancel. So you never need to click a circle more than once and the order does not matter (the test shuffled random click lists to check). The question becomes: which set of circles to click? Over the field of two elements this is a system of N linear equations in N unknowns.

Why M₁ must be odd, and why it is enough

With g = gcd(M, N), a block of M = g·M₁ neighbouring circles holds M₁ circles of each of the g classes of circles that are alike modulo g, and each class has N₁ = N/g circles. Every circle has to be flipped an odd number of times, so every class needs N₁ odd flips, an amount whose parity is that of N₁. But k clicks flip M₁·k circles of a class. So M₁·k ≡ N₁ (mod 2). Now M₁ and N₁ have no common factor, so they are not both even: if M₁ is even then N₁ is odd and M₁·k is even, which cannot equal it. No number of clicks works. If M₁ is odd, click every gth circle: each circle is then covered by exactly M₁ blocks, an odd number, so every circle turns blue, using N₁ clicks. The test replayed this for every pair with N up to 60. That N₁ clicks are the fewest was found by trying every set of circles (N up to 20) and by the equations over two elements (N up to 60, with the combinations of the kernel tried when it was small).

As in the applet, N runs from 5 to 24 and M from 2 to 12 (kept below N), a click changes M circles clockwise from the one clicked, and the puzzle is done when all the circles are blue. A white dot on a circle means you have clicked it an odd number of times.

Try N = 12 with M = 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8. Which can be done, in how many clicks, and what do their M₁ values say?
